title: What is the difference between String, StringBuilder, and StringBuffer?
shortTitle: What is the difference between String, StringBuilder, and StringBuffer?
keyPoints: String: immutable. Every modification creates a new object. Thread-safe by nature.
StringBuilder: mutable, NOT thread-safe. Fast for single-threaded string building.
StringBuffer: mutable, thread-safe (synchronized methods). Slower than StringBuilder.
Use StringBuilder for loops/concatenation in single-threaded code
Use StringBuffer only when multiple threads share the same builder (rare)
Since Java 9+, the compiler optimizes String + with invokedynamic, reducing the need for manual StringBuilder

s1_definition.oneliner: String is immutable (new object per change). StringBuilder is mutable and fast. StringBuffer is mutable and thread-safe (synchronized). Use StringBuilder by default.
s1_definition.profdef:
Three string types:

- **String:** Immutable. `s += "x"` creates a new String. Safe to share but slow for repeated modifications.
- **StringBuilder:** Mutable. Modifies in place without creating new objects. NOT thread-safe. Use for single-threaded building.
- **StringBuffer:** Mutable. Same API as StringBuilder but all methods are synchronized. Thread-safe but slower.
s1_definition.analogy: String is a printed bank statement – any change produces a new printout. StringBuilder is a whiteboard – erase and write freely, fast. StringBuffer is a whiteboard with a lock – only one person writes at a time, slower but safe.

sections.s3_flow:
```text
  String:        immutable, new object per change
  StringBuilder: mutable, not synchronized, fast
  StringBuffer:  mutable, synchronized, thread-safe, slow

  Loop:
    String +=    → N new objects → slow, GC pressure
    StringBuilder.append → 1 object, in-place → fast

  Rule: StringBuilder by default
        StringBuffer only for legacy multi-thread code
        String for simple values and constants
```
sections.s6_takeaway:
String is immutable – every modification creates a new object. StringBuilder is mutable and fast for single-threaded building. StringBuffer is mutable and thread-safe but slower. Use StringBuilder for loops and concatenation. Use StringBuffer only in legacy code that shares a builder across threads.

Since Java 9, simple `+` concatenation is optimized by the compiler. But in loops, StringBuilder is still essential.

One sentence to remember: String is immutable, StringBuilder is fast and mutable, StringBuffer adds synchronization – use StringBuilder by default.
